passage:
When Papa made the rule that my phone stays in the kitchen after ten, I didn't argue. I said "fine". Then I did everything he asked, just slowly. Emptying the dishwasher took forty minutes. I answered every question with "hmm" or "okay". When my brother Sumit asked if I wanted to play carrom, I said "no" and went back to my room to stare at the ceiling.
I thought I was being really mature, not shouting. Looking back, I was shouting, just quietly. Everyone could feel it.
On Sunday Papa sat on my bed and said, "You're allowed to be angry about the rule. I'd rather hear it than feel it." So I told him: my friends talk at night and I feel left out. We didn't scrap the rule, but we moved it to half past ten on weekends. I'm Mridul, fifteen, and I'm trying to use my words now.

qa.q: How long did Mridul take to empty the dishwasher?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did the slow chores and 'hmm' answers feel 'mature' to Mridul at the time?
qa.a: Not shouting felt grown-up, but Mridul was still angry about the rule, and the anger came out as quiet sulking.

qa.q: What choice of Papa's opened things up?
qa.a: Sitting on the bed and saying Mridul was allowed to be angry and he'd rather hear it, which led to a real talk and a weekend compromise.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Mridul refused to play carrom?
qa.a: Rejected and confused, caught in a mood that wasn't really about him.

grounding: A teenager who resents a new phone rule obeys with slow chores, scowls and one-word answers until a parent invites the anger out loud.

passage:
House-mother's note, Hostel B, Thursday
Since we brought in lights out at 10 p.m. for Class 11, Shalini has complied, in her own way. She switches off her lamp at 9:59 with a loud click. She takes twenty minutes to fold her uniform, scowling. When I say good morning, she says "morning" without looking up. Her roommate says she hasn't laughed all week.
I don't think Shalini is being defiant exactly. I think she's angry and doesn't see a safe way to say so. She is usually open and chatty.
Today I asked her to help me carry the laundry, and on the way I said, "I know you're not happy about lights out. Tell me what bothers you. I'd rather hear it than guess." She was quiet, then said she studies best late. We agreed she can use the common room till 10:30 twice a week before exams.
Kavitha, House-mother

qa.q: At what time does Shalini switch off her lamp?
qa.a: At 9:59, with a loud click.

qa.q: What does the loud click at 9:59 suggest Shalini is feeling?
qa.a: She is angry about the rule and shows it by obeying to the letter, since she doesn't see a safe way to say it directly.

qa.q: What choice of Kavitha's helped Shalini speak up?
qa.a: Inviting the complaint privately while they carried laundry, saying she'd rather hear it than guess, which made direct disagreement safe.

qa.q: How might Shalini's roommate experience this week?
qa.a: Probably tense and a bit gloomy, noticing Shalini hasn't laughed and unsure what's wrong.

grounding: A hostel house-mother notices a teenager obeying a new rule with scowls, slowness and monosyllables, and invites her to say her anger directly.

passage:
Saturday
Ma says I have to go to every single function of Seema Masi's daughter's wedding. All four days. Including the one on the night of my friend's birthday sleepover. I said "okay". I didn't say anything else all day.
I got ready for the haldi so slowly that Ma had to knock three times. I wore the orange suit she picked, but I scowled in every photo. When Masi asked if I was excited, I said "yes" like a robot. I ate one puri. I sat in the corner and answered my cousins with "hmm".
Here's the thing: I'm not actually mad at Masi. I'm mad at Ma for deciding without asking me. But if I say that, it'll turn into a big fight. So I'm being "obedient". Very, very slowly.
Maybe tomorrow I'll just tell Ma. Maybe.
Leela

qa.q: How many times did Ma have to knock while Leela got ready for the haldi?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Who is Leela really angry with, and why doesn't Leela say so?
qa.a: With Ma, for deciding without asking; Leela fears saying it will start a big fight, so the anger comes out as slow, silent obedience. 😠

qa.q: What could Leela try tomorrow instead of the slow scowl?
qa.a: Tell Ma calmly that deciding without asking hurt, and ask whether there's any room to talk about the birthday night.

qa.q: How might Seema Masi feel when Leela says 'yes' like a robot?
qa.a: Maybe hurt or confused, thinking Leela doesn't care about the wedding, when the anger isn't about Masi at all.

grounding: A teenager who resents being made to attend every wedding function complies with scowls, slowness and one-word answers.

passage:
Since Papa made the new rule, that Eshaan must help at the hardware shop in Chhindwara every Sunday instead of playing cricket, Eshaan, fourteen, had not argued once.
He came at nine sharp. He stood behind the counter with his jaw set. When Papa asked him to sort the screws by size, he picked them up one at a time, turned each over, and dropped it into the tin as if it weighed a kilo. A twenty-minute job took two hours. A customer asked for a hinge; Eshaan pointed at the shelf without a word.
"Everything okay?" Papa asked.
"Hmm."
"Hungry?"
"No."
His older cousin Mridul, who worked there on weekdays, leaned over while Papa was at the back. "You're allowed to be angry about the cricket, you know. You could just say it."
Eshaan kept dropping screws, one by one.

qa.q: How long did the screw-sorting job take?
qa.a: Two hours, for a twenty-minute job.

qa.q: What is Eshaan feeling as he drops each screw "as if it weighed a kilo"?
qa.a: He is angry and resentful about losing Sunday cricket, but shows it through slowness and silence rather than saying so.

qa.q: What could Eshaan try instead of the slow sorting?
qa.a: Telling Papa directly that missing cricket feels unfair and asking whether Sunday afternoons or another day could work instead.

qa.q: Why might Mridul say, "You could just say it"?
qa.a: Mridul can see the anger behind the silence and seems to think an honest word would be easier on everyone, Eshaan included, than hours of sulking.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who resents a new Sunday rule obeying with a set jaw, doing the work at a crawl and answering in grunts, his anger disguised as compliance.
